description: Palestinian Football Association (PFA) President Jibril Rajoub criticised the United States and Canada after he and members of the Palestinian football delegation were reportedly denied visas to attend FIFA events and World Cup matches in North America. 
Rajoub said during an interview in Mexico City on Friday that he had applied to attend several matches and next week's FIFA summit in Miami, but had yet to receive approval, adding that other federation officials, referees, athletes and employees had also been refused visas. 
"This is not good for the sport. This is also not good for the hosting countries," he asserted, noting that Canada likewise denied his application, calling it 'a violation of their commitment' to ensure "they will facilitate and they will not deny a visa to any relevant person, to the sport or to the family of football." 
Asked whether the refusals were linked to his position, Rajoub declined to speculate and instead argued that the spirit of the World Cup should guarantee access for everyone connected to the game. 
The PFA president also revealed that he remains in contact with FIFA Chief Gianni Infantino, stressing that responsibility lies with the host governments. 
"He is trying and he will keep his efforts to try to overcome this challenge," Rajoub declared, persisting, "He is not responsible and he should not be blamed. Those who should be blamed – the relevant governments of the countries hosting," Rajoub underscored. 
He argued that the refusals are '100 percent' contrary to "the rules, the spirit, the commitment, the aspirations" of international sport and maintained that host nations have an obligation to facilitate participation by members of the global football community. 
He also called on FIFA and UEFA to sanction the Israeli Football Association over alleged violations of FIFA statutes and the Olympic Charter, insisting, "The double standard policy should stop. The sanctions should be imposed." 
Despite his criticism, Rajoub congratulated the United States, Canada and Mexico on hosting the tournament while expressing regret that he and others had been unable to attend 'this historic and international event'. 
The 2026 FIFA World Cup, running from 11 June to 19 July, is the first edition to feature 48 teams and the first to be jointly hosted by the United States, Canada and Mexico, with matches taking place across 16 cities in North America.

description: The DRC's national football team, which secured the country's first FIFA World Cup qualification in 52 years, has become a symbol of hope for residents of Goma, who have been dealing with a recent Ebola outbreak and violence between armed groups affecting the region. 
Footage filmed on Friday shows signs featuring information on Ebola prevention, DRC national team jerseys displayed in local stores, and a local squad practising. 
"It's a huge relief for the people of eastern Congo who were facing war. Now they'll have their eyes glued to the United States, Canada, or Mexico to follow the World Cup," said Ben Muhima, a sports analyst. 
He explained, "In Beni, we talk about the massacres, but everyone will stop, everyone will forget those massacres, and everyone will be on the side of the United States to support the Leopards." 
Charles Mbuyi, coach of the MGL-Goma Football Academy, shared that he believes the Leopards are capable of challenging Portugal when the two sides meet in their opening World Cup match. 
Another academy coach, Ngulu Robert, stressed football has become an important source of hope for local people. 
"It makes us forget about war and the Ebola disease. Thank God, after 52 years, we've qualified for the World Cup. May this not be the first or last time we qualify," he detailed. 
Members of Goma's football community said qualifying after more than five decades was a source of pride for a generation that had never seen the country compete at the World Cup, noting that the US government's visa restrictions on the DRC's population are disappointing. 
"I wasn't even born yet, but I'm happy because it brings us joy, especially since we're in a red zone," declared Amani Gaston. 
The DRC is in Group K alongside Portugal, Uzbekistan, and Colombia.

description: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said a proposed two-phase agreement between Iran and the United States could bring an end to ongoing hostilities and pave the way for negotiations on Tehran's nuclear programme and sanctions relief.

"In these negotiations, which will lead to the end of the war, two phases have been envisioned. The first phase is a memorandum of understanding to be signed between Iran and the US, after which negotiations for the second phase will begin," he said.

The minister added that a second phase would consist of 60 days of negotiations aimed at reaching a comprehensive agreement covering more contentious issues.

"Then, in the second phase, we will have a final agreement. We have postponed the nuclear issue to the final agreement for various reasons, as it was truly impossible to discuss it under the current circumstances," he added.

Araghchi noted that the war should end on all fronts, including in Lebanon.

"I have said this many times: we have never forgotten Lebanon in this war, because Lebanon and Hezbollah, in any case, fought alongside the people of Iran in this war, and we will never abandon them. The ceasefire that was announced was also for all fronts, including Lebanon," he explained.

He said future negotiations would focus on uranium enrichment and Iran's stockpiles of enriched material, which he said are the most difficult issues still to be resolved.

"Of course, our position has always been, and it has been our logical stance, that if these are to be decided upon, in our view, the only method for high-level enriched materials, specifically the 60 percent materials, is their dilution within Iran," he added.

Araghchi also stated the agreement would provide for the release of Iranian assets frozen abroad and include commitments prohibiting threats or the use of force.

"Iran's blocked assets will also be released according to the memorandum of understanding that will be signed," he assured.
 
The foreign minister also warned that opponents of the agreement could attempt to undermine the process.

"I must explicitly state that this agreement has enemies, at the forefront of which is the Zionist regime, and they are looking for pretexts to disrupt this agreement," he said, identifying Israel as the primary opponent and accusing it of seeking opportunities to derail negotiations.

Araghchi argued that threats and military pressure would not alter Iran's position.

"In these circumstances, threats are not only ineffective but also set back a potential agreement; threats must stop, and we must speak with the language of respect in order for us to reach an agreement," he said. 

Donald Trump announced on Thursday that a deal with Iran could be signed 'this weekend... maybe in Europe' - but added that there wasn't a deadline.

Trump earlier announced he had 'cancelled' another attack on Iran, after the sides exchanged strikes the previous evening - and also earlier in the week following the Apache helicopter crash, which the US blamed on an Iranian drone.

description: Workers at floriculture company Naranjo Roses in Tanicuchi handcraft floral arrangements inspired by the flags of the 48 national teams participating in the 2026 FIFA World Cup. 
Footage shows workers handcrafting intricate floral arrangements and national flags from locally grown flowers, showcasing the craftsmanship behind a project that blends the country's renowned floriculture industry with the world's biggest football tournament.
"Naranjo Roses produces approximately 35 million stems per year, of which two million stems are destined for preserved roses, including stems and buds," explained Juan Carlos Yancha, operations and quality manager.
The arrangements seek to pay tribute to the cultural diversity that characterises the World Cup and, at the same time, promote the quality of Ecuadorian floriculture on the international stage.
"We offer all countries, the most requested are from South America and obviously Ecuador, because it is in the World Cup," said Giovanni Sarosoza, supervisor of dyed roses.
The preserved roses undergo a lengthy production process that includes harvesting, cultivation, bleaching and dyeing before being assembled into the finished designs. According to the company, each piece takes 10 to 12 days to complete, and its durability depends largely on the customer's care. 
"It lasts from two to three years, but if you take even more care of it, it can last longer," remarked Erika Imacana, rose supervisor. 
Ecuador is one of the world's leading exporters of roses, with the high-altitude climate around Tanicuchi providing ideal growing conditions. By combining one of the country's signature products with football's biggest event, the company hopes its floral creations will reach customers well beyond the World Cup itself.

description: Families gathered in Ahmedabad on Friday to mark one year since the Air India Flight AI171 crash that killed 260 people, with many calling for answers as the investigation into the disaster remains incomplete. 
Footage shows around 150 relatives gathering with portraits of their loved ones for the ceremony. The crowd later assembled near the Meghaninagar crash site, offering floral tributes and lighting candles in silent remembrance. 
During the ceremony, President of the Federation of Indian Pilots Captain CS Randhawa criticised what he described as inadequate support for bereaved families. 
"It was so painful to hear what they have undergone after the crash to collect even the dead bodies of their loved ones," Randhawa said. "There is nil support after a few months after the crash and until today the airline has not been interacting with the families." 
The London-bound Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner went down shortly after take-off on June 12, 2025. The aircraft crashed into the BJ Medical College hostel complex, killing 241 people on board and 19 people on the ground. 
Randhawa said investigators were still examining multiple possibilities before publishing their final findings, but disputed suggestions of pilot error. 
"Main reason for this crash, we have ruled out any pilot error. This is mainly due to the electrical problems in the aircraft, which have been persistent. There have been a lot of problems in the aircraft," he asserted. 
Patel Anil Kumar Ambala, father of one of the victims, said grieving families were still waiting for definitive answers and justice as questions remain over what caused the disaster. 
"No report has been given yet. We don't even know how the plane crash happened. We want justice for this incident. We are demanding it. We are also appealing to the government to give us justice for it, whatever report comes," Ambala said. 
"It has been almost a year. Still no report, nothing is known, so we are a bit angry with the government. We can say this. Whatever report the government has, it should be cleared quickly," he added. 
The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau's preliminary report found both engine fuel control switches moved from "RUN" to "CUTOFF" seconds after take-off, cutting fuel to the engines. Investigators have not determined what caused the switches to change position. 
On the anniversary, the AAIB said the investigation had entered its final analysis stage and urged restraint over speculation while technical examinations continue with international partners.

Trade unions argue that without substantial state intervention to lower soaring energy costs and counter cheap Asian imports, the survival of Europe's heavy manufacturing sector remains uncertain.

The Pact officially entered into force on June 12, although member states are expected to continue adapting their administrative and operational systems in the coming months with support from the European Union Agency for Asylum. 
According to EU officials, the new framework introduces mandatory registration, security and vulnerability checks for people entering the bloc irregularly, while creating faster procedures for processing asylum claims and returns. 
Human rights groups and NGOs have also expressed concern that the legislation could expand the use of detention for asylum seekers at the EU's external borders, including for families and, in some circumstances, children.

The Medical Director of La Citadelle Clinic, Dr Sila Jakwong'a, shared that the 25-year-old student died suddenly before her Ebola test results arrived. 
"It's heartbreaking to see people die, sometimes in the difficult conditions they work in. We can't eliminate that, but it's truly painful. "Now that it's already attacking our loved ones, we see that it's really the reality. The disease is here and it's real, and it often kills our loved ones, our families, the people we live with, and it hurts us deeply. Right now, we too are afraid," he said. 
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, was officially declared by the DRC on 15 May after cases were identified in the Bunia, Rwampara and Mongbwalu health zones. 
The WHO says there is currently no licensed vaccine or specific treatment for this strain. 
According to the latest figures released this week, the DRC has recorded nearly 600 confirmed cases and at least 115 deaths, with the vast majority concentrated in Ituri Province. 
The WHO and Africa CDC recently launched a $518 million continental response plan to support containment measures.

Israel intercepted the Global Sumud Flotilla in international waters last month, seizing all 50 vessels and detaining 428 participants from more than 40 countries. 
The convoy aimed to deliver humanitarian aid to Gaza amid Israel's ongoing land and naval blockade, with the enclave facing severe shortages of food, medicine, and essential supplies. 
The interceptions and detentions sparked strong backlash worldwide and in Israel, after Ben-Gvir posted footage on social media of him taunting blindfolded, bound, and kneeling detainees at Ashdod Port. 
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defended Israel's right to stop the flotilla but criticised Ben-Gvir, saying the way he dealt with the activists was 'not in line with Israel's values'.bus

description: Outgoing US Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard claimed that previous US administrations had lied about the existence and funding of biolabs - including in Ukraine - in a bombshell statement on Friday.

"Until now, evidence regarding the full existence and funding of these laboratories had been knowingly withheld from you, the American people. Many of these US government funded bio labs are currently or have previously engaged in research using hazardous and highly contagious pathogens, and in some cases included dangerous gain of function research with very little visibility or oversight," she said.

Donald Trump signed an executive order ending funding for 'gain of function' research last year - a type of science that alters an organism's or pathogen's genetic code to give it new abilities or enhance existing traits.

"Despite the obvious potential for catastrophic global impact, that research on dangerous pathogens and bio labs can have, politicians and so-called health professionals like Doctor Fauci, as well as entities within the Biden administration's national security team, lied repeatedly to the American people about the existence of U.S. funded and supported bio labs," she went on.

"Not only did they lie, they threatened those who attempted to expose the truth, she went on. So this release today breaks new ground as the information surrounding the existence, history, locations, and funding of these US funded bio labs has been intentionally covered up by very powerful people who falsely claimed that these bio labs didn't exist. Now, they accused anyone who says otherwise to be foreign assets and traitors to America".

Slides released - and also available on this site -  include confirmation of over 40 such labs in Ukraine - and the startling revelation that those labs included "Anthrax, tularemia, tuberculosis, Swine Fever, New Castles Disease, MERS, SARS, Marburg, Ebola, Lassa, the Plague [and] Rickettsia."

The slides also confirmed a list of connections between the Ukrainian lab and the US Biowarfare defence industry. Ukraine has not commented, while Russia has repeatedly accused the US of funding such biolabs. The US has previously confirmed 'public health laboratories' for the 'safe handling of pathogens' and preventing disease outbreaks.

Gabbard is stepping down from her role as of June 30, citing her husband's recent cancer diagnosis.

The Canary Islands remain one of the main gateways into Spain for migrants attempting the Atlantic crossing from West Africa. A record 46,843 migrants arrived in the archipelago in 2024, before numbers declined in 2025. 
The visit to Las Raices was one of the final major engagements of Pope Leo's seven-day trip to Spain, during which migration remained a central theme.

description: A two-year-old white Pomeranian named Haku has made history in Japan by becoming the first dog of his breed to join a police force. 
Footage filmed on Thursday in the Miyazaki Prefecture shows Haku taking part in training exercises, weaving through obstacles, and responding to commands alongside his handlers. 
According to police dog trainer Hikaru Takekoshi, Haku's path to police work began as an effort to correct behavioural problems rather than prepare him for service. 
"He barked excessively and was a bit unruly and disobedient, so he was entrusted to us for training as a pet dog," she said. 
"As we continued training, we gradually began to see his high abilities. So, when we mentioned that he might even be able to become a police dog, the owner said, 'Well, if he has that kind of ability, then I'd really like you to help him develop it,'" she continued. 
Police dogs in Japan are traditionally larger breeds such as German Shepherds and Labradors, but Takekoshi said ability matters more than size. 
"Especially during a disaster, in collapsed houses or other structures, large dogs can be heavy, and it can be dangerous for them to move around," she noted. 
"In narrow gaps that are inaccessible due to collapse, small dogs can use their agility and small size to search effectively," she added. 
Haku's appointment could open the door for more dogs of different breeds and sizes to take on specialist roles, particularly in disaster zones where agility and access to confined spaces can prove crucial.

Widely known as Princess Bha, she collapsed while training dogs for an army exhibition in Nakhon Ratchasima province in December 2022. The palace later said she had suffered a severe heart arrhythmia following a mycoplasma infection. 
The Princess had remained in a coma ever since – more than three years – receiving treatment at King Chulalongkorn Memorial Hospital.  
A palace update in May said doctors had detected an abdominal infection caused by inflammation of the large intestine. Her condition had become unstable, with low blood pressure, an irregular heartbeat and blood‑clotting abnormalities. 
Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul described her death as an “immeasurable grief in the hearts of the entire nation”, praising her contribution to public service. 
Her death also removes one of the Thai royal family’s most experienced and popular public figures. A 1974 amendment to the constitution allows a woman to take the Thai throne, so Princess Bajrakitiyabha had long been seen as a possible successor or as a regent to help Prince Dipangkorn Rasmijoti after their father’s death.

description: European Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner was asked about claims the bloc's new migration pact was the 'end of humanity in Europe' as he arrived for informal talks on the agreement in  Nicosia on Friday.

 "What do you say to the criticism from NGOs who say, today is the end of humanity in Europe, and with the new asylum system, fundamental rights are being restricted?" he was asked.

"It's exactly the opposite. For the first time, we can say we are actually saving lives because we are also preventing people from embarking on this dangerous journey that often ends in death across the Mediterranean, across the Atlantic. And we have many red lines as well. Of course, human rights must be respected," he claimed.

He was also asked about huge divisions in the bloc over the new rules.

"What do you do with member states like Hungary or Poland that are not really willing to cooperate on certain aspects?" the reporter put to him.

"I think more likely, for example, if certain things need to be adjusted technically in IT, if there is still something infrastructure-wise that needs to be done. So there are different challenges for the member states. Not everyone has the same challenges. And to support here, that is our job, to support the member states so that it works," he added.

The EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, a major overhaul of the system, was introduced by 'qualified majority', with Poland, Hungary and Slovakia voting against.

Poland and Hungary have argued for national responsibility for migration - and have hit out at the 'solidarity pool' detailed in the agreement which shares numbers across the bloc. Nations can accept their 'share', or pay for others to take their share, or provide 'operational support'.

The agreement comes into force on June 12 and also includes sped-up deportations, and potential third country 'return hubs'. Critics have accused the EU of weakening asylum protections and attempting to create a 'fortress' to avoid taking responsibility for those fleeing conflict while supporters say it creates one unified system.

Authorities said all employees and on-site personnel were safely evacuated, with no injuries reported. 
Officials also confirmed that the fire did not pose a threat to nearby residential areas, while crews continued efforts to bring the blaze under control and assess the extent of the damage.

description: Rescuers on the Russian island of Sakhalin removed a plastic noose from the neck of an endangered Steller sea lion, after the 230-kilogramme creature was seen struggling to breathe and unable to swallow food. 
As the sea lion grew, the plastic ring dug ever deeper into its throat, leaving it facing a slow and painful death.
Footage shot on Wednesday shows the team approaching the herd and subduing the injured sea lion with an anaesthetic dart. The rescuers then cut off the plastic waste from around its neck and treated its wounds. The video also shows an enormous and decidedly angry seal approaching the intrepid medics, having misunderstood their intentions toward its pal, but they remained undaunted and continued their life-saving operation.
The press office of the Sakhalin region government added that this was the first time that sea lions had been rescued directly from a breakwater in Russia.
"We assessed the situation, arrived at the location, selected the target animal, re-assessed it, estimated its weight and calculated the anaesthetic dose required. <...> We fired the shot and the animal went down after 13 minutes. Thirty minutes after the shot, we approached and removed the packing tape - collar, which was constricting the animal’s neck. <...> We waited, and the animal woke up. Everything was fine," explained Maria Chistyayeva, chief veterinarian at the Primorsky Aquarium. 
She added that the problem most likely arose because the cub had been playing with the plastic ring, which then became stuck around its neck.
Minister for Environment and Sustainable Development of the Sakhalin region Andrei Samatov reported that the two injured animals had been discovered by tourists. The operation to rescue the second Steller sea lion will take place next week.
"A decision was made to try to help the animals. A preliminary inspection was therefore carried out last week to determine the number of animals affected. <...> They would have died in the near future," he noted.
The operation involved federal and regional experts, as well as other institutions and non-governmental organisations in the Sakhalin region. It will serve as a reference for future interventions in emergency cases involving the endangered species.

description: With the 2026 FIFA World Cup already underway, a street in the city of Novo Hamburgo, in southern Brazil, became a symbol of Carioca soccer passion thanks to a monumental mural approximately 200 meters long dedicated to player Neymar.

"Our expectation for this World Cup is that the sixth title will come to our country and that we will be able to celebrate it next month, in the final," Carvalho added.

World Cup street paintings are part of a tradition that goes back several decades in Brazil. Residents decorate entire streets with the national colours of green and yellow, drawings of players and messages of support for the national team.

description: Colombian presidential candidate Ivan Cepeda announced on Thursday that he filed a 'criminal complaint' before the Office of the Attorney General and the International Criminal Court (ICC) against his opponent Abelardo de la Espriella, whom he links to paramilitary groups that operated in the country.  
At a press conference in Bogota, he reported that the complaint is based on alleged crimes of criminal conspiracy, financing of terrorism, and illicit enrichment, which, he said, would be related to crimes against humanity committed by structures of the now-defunct United Self-Defence Forces of Colombia (AUC). 
The candidate indicated that the legal action includes 'new elements' that emerged in judicial proceedings, investigations, and truth clarification mechanisms developed in recent years. 
"I clarify that this action is not a repetition of other criminal actions that have been undertaken in the past against De la Espriella, since our written complaint includes new elements that have appeared over time," he stated. 
Cepeda claimed that the new evidence could help clarify the extent of De la Espriella's relationship with the AUC, demobilised in the mid-2000s. 
He also asked that previous investigations be reopened and requested the ICC's intervention, as the reported events may constitute crimes under international jurisdiction. 
"In this complaint, proceedings are being brought for three crimes associated with crimes against humanity committed by paramilitary structures belonging to the United Self-Defence Forces of Colombia, and those crimes are three," he said, citing criminal conspiracy, financing of terrorism, and illicit enrichment.
De la Espriella denied previous allegations linking him to paramilitary groups, and no court established criminal responsibility in relation to the claims raised by Cepeda.
The announcement comes 10 days before the Colombian presidential runoff, scheduled for June 21, amid a campaign marked by mutual accusations between the candidates.

video211
description: Fans with hearing and visual impairments were able to enjoy the opening match of the FIFA 2026 World Cup, thanks to the help of professional interpreters using sign language and tactile sign language to help them follow clash between Mexico and South Africa in Guadalajara. 

The interpretation work was carried out by specialists such as Omar Martinez, who explained the importance of creating accessible spaces for such vital international events.
 
"What we are doing today is interpretation for deaf people and for a deafblind person, in which we use tactile sign language, where the deaf person touches the hands and can understand the interpretation and what is happening in the match," he explained. 

The initiative allowed fans with disabilities to follow every play and share in the emotions of the match. 

One of the attendees was Jose de Jesus Loera, who was born deaf or hard of hearing before later completely losing his sight. He explained that this was his first experience a World Cup match. 

"I feel more emotions, with the vibration, with the speakers and the screen. I feel that it is much more exciting," he said. 

Among the other attendees was Manuel Martinez Garcia, who is hearing impaired. He highlighted the value of taking part in a sporting event, free from communication barriers, as part of an inclusive community. 

"It gives me more emotions to see that there are many people and to be with all the people so that we are not excluded. It's very exciting to feel it, and I hope Mexico wins," he added. 

The activity was part of FutFest 2026, a programme promoted by the University of Guadalajara to bring the World Cup closer to the population through free broadcasts, cultural activities, and inclusion initiatives. 

The main venue was the Bicentenario Screen at the University Cultural Centre, considered one of the most important public spaces in the state.

description: Thousands of fans gathered this Thursday at the Angel of Independence in Mexico City to celebrate Mexico's 2-0 victory over South Africa in the opening match of the FIFA World Cup 2026. 
Footage shows Mexican supporters wearing jerseys, waving flags, chanting, singing, and dancing after the national team secured its first-ever World Cup win in an opener.
Despite rain falling across parts of the capital, hundreds of fans remained in the streets to continue the celebrations after the victory at Estadio Ciudad de Mexico. 
Attendees reported optimism regarding the Mexican national team's performance, though some fans noted areas for improvement. 
Emmanuel Villalobos said the match was 'very good' but added, "I think some things were missing to sort out there on the wings. Better finishing is needed. There are many opportunities that need to be taken next time."
Supporter Armando Zepeda shared that he would have liked a wider scoreline, especially given Mexico's numerical advantage during part of the match.
"I feel that Mexico did a good job. But there are many things to improve," he said, persisting, "Two extra men and not taking advantage of it, well, but against Korea it is going to improve a lot, and I am sure we are going for the nine points, and we are going to qualify."
Authorities closed roads around the Angel of Independence to accommodate the crowds, with celebrations continuing peacefully throughout the afternoon.
Mexico is one of the three host countries of the FIFA World Cup 2026, along with the United States and Canada, in the largest edition in the tournament's history, featuring 48 national teams. 
After its victory over South Africa, the Mexican national team will return to action on June 18 to face South Korea in Guadalajara on the second matchday of Group A.

description: Thousands of fans celebrated in the streets around Mexico City Stadium in Mexico City's Tlalpan borough on Thursday after Mexico defeated South Africa in the opening match of the 2026 FIFA World Cup.
Supporters gathered along Calzada de Tlalpan and around the Mercado de Huipulco area, where celebrations continued for several hours after the final whistle. Footage shows fans chanting, singing, and waving Mexican flags as green, white, and red flares lit up the night sky to mark the host nation's 2-0 victory.
The victory sparked scenes of jubilation among supporters, many of whom expressed hope that the national team can go further than in previous World Cup campaigns.
"Hopefully they stay on that good path and make it to the fifth match, which they have not reached," commented Luis Angel Morales, a fan. 
For Ivan Morales, the celebrations were about more than just the result, offering a chance to share his passion for football and mark a historic day for Mexican sport.
"I am having a good time. I came because I love football, I love my city, I love Mexico. So to support in every way possible," he said. 
Despite the victory, some supporters voiced there was still room for improvement ahead of Mexico's remaining group-stage matches.
"They played well today, but in the end it kind of disappointed us a little," remarked a fan, Ivan Morales, asserting, "But yes, there goes Mexico, there it goes little by little, Mexico."
Families, groups of friends and visitors from across Mexico and abroad joined the post-match celebrations, reflecting the excitement generated by both the start of the World Cup and the host nation's winning start to the tournament.

"May the celebration continue to be seen this way," the Colombian added.

"I believe there is a lot of motivation from being in the country, and the truth is that there are many young people with a lot of talent, and we expect something very good for them," she said.

description: The 2026 FIFA World Cup officially kicked off on Thursday, with the Capitol in Washington DC becoming one of the central gathering points for fans. 
Footage shows crowds filling designated viewing areas and watching the Mexico-South Africa match on large outdoor screens. The game ended with a 2-0 win for Mexico.

video217
description: The first group of Nigerians voluntarily evacuated from South Africa arrived in Lagos on Thursday, as concerns grow over anti-migrant sentiment and reports of discrimination against foreign nationals. 
Footage shows returning citizens, including women and children, being welcomed by authorities before proceeding with registration processes. 
The returnees highlighted the difficulties they faced while living in South Africa, and what they described as growing levels of discrimination. 
"The problem in South Africa is with the leaders," said returnee Emeka Obodo. "They have literally made everybody an illegal immigrant in their country. When you seek a document, they will not give it to you, and when you go to process it, they will arrest you." 
"Xenophobia did not really affect me personally, but it affected my child. Teachers discriminated against him and were biased towards him," shared Millie Abu, a mother of three. 
Patience Chime, a mother of four, said worsening conditions left her family with little choice but to return home. 
"They asked us to leave," she said. They stopped us from doing our business. They said we must not do business. That was why we decided to come back to Nigeria." 
Meanwhile, the Nigerian authorities said efforts are now focused on helping returnees reintegrate into society. 
"Some of these children have to go to school. There is a lot of work to be done with state and local governments on how to reintegrate their citizens, but the President has done the biggest thing, which is to pay for their flight to come back home," said Abike Dabiri, CEO of the Nigerians in Diaspora Commission. 
In recent months, South Africa has seen a surge in anti-immigrant protests, fuelled by anger over unemployment, poverty and pressure on public services. Ghana, Nigeria, Malawi and Mozambique have moved to repatriate affected citizens after recent xenophobic attacks. 
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has commissioned five emergency government-funded evacuation flights to repatriate over 1,000 Nigerian nationals from South Africa. The first flight brought home 262 passengers along with three government officials on Thursday morning. 
President Cyril Ramaphosa has warned against vigilante action, saying 'there is no space for xenophobia, racism, sexism, Afrophobia or any other forms of intolerance' in South Africa.

The incident occurred as members of the ultra-Orthodox Jewish community blocked highways in several cities across Israel.
On Wednesday, the Knesset voted 56–43 to advance the 'Basic Law Proposal: Torah Study' bill to a preliminary reading, which would allow ultra-Orthodox Jewish men to avoid military conscription. Despite the bill's progress, protesters continued to block highways for several hours, Israeli media reported.
Members of the Haredi community have been exempted from military service in Israel; however, a Supreme Court ruling in 2024 declared this blanket exemption unconstitutional.
The bill proposes to enshrine in a basic law the status of Torah study as a fundamental value in the heritage of the Jewish people.
To become law, the bill requires three additional readings in the Knesset plenum, along with rigorous debate and preparation in the relevant parliamentary committees.

The operation, known as 'Last Mile', establishes a controlled access perimeter around the stadium to manage the arrival of fans and strengthen security during tournament matches.

Many fans said the heightened security was noticeable but well organised.

"There are quite a lot of security checkpoints. We had to walk several kilometres but here we are. We hope it will be a great celebration - I know the whole world is waiting for it," said Luz Quintero.

Traffic restrictions were introduced in stages from the night before the match, while security personnel set up checkpoints on the main routes leading to the stadium.

Within the security perimeter, access is limited to ticket holders, accredited residents, authorised vehicles, as well as emergency and security services.

"We went through the security checkpoint with the police. [...] Super calm, safe. Police officers and train cars at every point. The streets are calm while walking," noted Jose Brito, another fan.

The operation forms part of a wider mobility and security plan for the tournament, which Mexico is hosting alongside the United States and Canada. 

Restrictions will remain in place throughout the day and are expected to be used again for the remaining World Cup fixtures scheduled at the stadium.

Mexico City is one of the main host cities for the FIFA World Cup 2026 and is staging the tournament's opening match between Mexico and South Africa, along with several other fixtures.

The 2026 World Cup will be the first edition staged across three countries. It will also be the largest of its kind in history, featuring 48 national teams and 104 matches.

description: Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, confirmed that the Governing Council had raised eurozone interest rates by 25 basis points - the first rise since 2023 - blaming inflation shockwaves from the Middle East crisis on Thursday.
 
"The governing council is committed to setting monetary policy to ensure that inflation stabilises at our two per cent target in the medium term. In line with this commitment, we today decided to raise the three key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points," she said.

"The war in the Middle East is generating inflation pressures, and the decision to raise rates is robust across a range of scenarios, mapping out how the shock might evolve and affect the medium-term outlook for the euro area," she added.

The bank hiked the key interest rate to 2.25 per cent, downgrading the growth forecast too.
shotlist: *NO CUTAWAYS AT SOURCE*
SOT, Christine Lagarde, President of the European Central Bank (English): "The governing council is committed to setting monetary policy to ensure that inflation stabilises at our two per cent target in the medium term. In line with this commitment, we today decided to raise the three key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points. The war in the Middle East is generating inflation pressures, and the decision to raise rates is robust across a range of scenarios, mapping out how the shock might evolve and affect the medium-term outlook for the euro area." SOT, Christine Lagarde, President of the European Central Bank (English): "The outlook remains uncertain, with upside risks for inflation and downside risks for economic growth. The full implication of the war for medium-term inflation and growth will depend on the intensity and duration of the energy price shock as well as the scale of its indirect and second round effects." SOT, Christine Lagarde, President of the European Central Bank (English): "Let me first look at the economic activity. Adjusting for a temporary factor in Ireland, the euro area economy grew in the first quarter, supported by domestic demand and exports. Yet the war in the Middle East is weighing on activity and surveys are pointing to a slowdown, especially in services. Manufacturing has held up so far. In part, this is because firms have been building up stocks to cope with supply chain pressures. It also reflects higher defence spending. The labour market remains resilient. Unemployment at 6.3 per cent in April remains close to historical lows. The first quarter saw additional jobs being created, although at a slower pace than in the last quarter in 2025. Labour demand has cooled further, and firms and households expect the labour market to weaken. Looking ahead, staff now expect domestic demand to be weaker than they projected in March as the war weighs on confidence and higher energy costs erode real incomes. At the same time, household balance sheets are solid overall and consumption should remain the main driver of growth. Higher energy costs and lower confidence will dent private investment in the short run, but it should be underpinned by firms investing in new digital technologies. Governments spending more on defence and infrastructure should continue to support public investments. These factors are expected to provide some cushioning against the fallout from the war." SOT, Christine Lagarde, President of the European Central Bank (English): "The risks now to the inflation outlook are to the upside. If energy prices were to rise by more and for longer than currently expected, euro area inflation would increase further. This could be reinforced and become more persistent if higher energy prices were to spill over by more than expected to other prices and to wages, if longer term inflation expectations were to rise in response or if global supply chains were disrupted more broadly." SOT, Christine Lagarde, President of the European Central Bank (English): "Euro area banks are resilient, supported by strong capital and liquidity ratios, solid asset quality and robust profitability. However, a sudden sharp drop in asset prices, potentially amplified by the non-bank financial sector and deteriorating asset quality, particularly in energy and trade sensitive sectors, would pose risks to financial stability. These risks increase the longer the current geopolitical conflicts last. Macroprudential policy remains the first line of defence against the build-up of financial vulnerabilities, enhancing resilience and preserving macroprudential space. So in conclusion, the Governing Council today decided to raise the three key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points. We are committed to setting monetary policy to ensure that inflation stabilises at our two per cent target in the medium term. We will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary policy stance. Our interest rate decisions will be based on our assessment of the inflation outlook and the risks surrounding it in light of the incoming economic and financial data, as well as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission. We are not pre-committing to a particular rate path. In any case, we stand ready to adjust all of our instruments within our mandate to ensure that inflation stabilises sustainably at our medium-term target and to preserve the smooth functioning of monetary policy transmission." SOT, Christine Lagarde, President of the European Central Bank (English): "If you look at our monetary policy statement, we say very specifically that with this 25 basis point increase of interest rates we are well positioned to navigate the uncertainty and the developments going forward. So, that stands very clearly in the MPS. As to the rest, we will be deciding meeting by meeting. We will be data dependent. We will have no preset, predetermined rate path going forward. And that's the way we will be operating."

description: With Los Angeles preparing to host eight matches during the 2026 FIFA World Cup, the city's homelessness crisis remains one of its most visible challenges - and tens of thousands of people across the county still on the streets.

Footage shows rows of tents and makeshift shelters lining a street in Los Angeles, with piles of rubbish bags stacked nearby, Rough sleepers can be seen sitting among their belongings, moving between tents and shopping trolleys.

However, the city's growing network of tiny home villages - prefab housing for rough sleepers - such as Alexandria Park Tiny Home Village, is going someway to helping. The small prefabricated units offer a private space, a bed, a lockable door and access to support services while residents wait for permanent housing.

"It’s not perfect, but you have a bed, you have your own space, and you don’t have to worry about someone taking your stuff," said Alexandria Park resident Martha Stahley.

"As far as people dealing with substance abuse, they have support services in place. They help residents make appointments and even assist them in getting there, to help them avoid returning to the streets."

In recent years, Los Angeles has invested heavily in interim housing, including hotel rooms and tiny home villages, as part of Mayor Karen Bass's effort to reduce homelessness. According to media reports, thousands of people are now living in city-backed tiny homes across Los Angeles.

Yet even supporters say the programme remains too small to meet demand. Despite the expansion of temporary accommodation, an estimated 72,000 people remain unhoused across Los Angeles County - and will continue to be long after the World Cup circus has moved on.

video260
description: A sharp rise in soybean prices is squeezing Indonesia's tofu and tempeh producers, forcing many small businesses to cut product sizes, reduce output and scale back operations as the weakening rupiah drives up import costs.

Footage shows workers at a tofu factory in Sawangan, West Java, grinding soybeans, processing curds and shaping blocks of tofu ready for distribution to local markets.

Indonesia relies heavily on imported soybeans for tofu and tempeh production, leaving manufacturers exposed to currency fluctuations and global commodity price movements. As the US dollar strengthens against the rupiah, the cost of imported soybeans has climbed, eroding already thin profit margins.

“To be honest, the spike in soybean prices has had a massive impact. Prices have gone up by nearly 30 percent. Since Ramadan, the price has surged from 8,500 IDR ($0.47) per kg to 11,200 IDR ($0.62) today,” said factory owner Nasirin.

“This situation puts me, as a tofu factory owner, in a real dilemma. If we make the tofu pieces smaller, customers complain. But if we stick to our standard size, we lose money. I just want the government to step in and handle this situation.”

The government has responded with emergency measures aimed at stabilising supplies of the staple protein products. The Ministry for Food Affairs authorised a Rp 2,000 subsidy per kilogram of soybeans through the state logistics agency, Bulog, and set a price ceiling of Rp 11,500 per kilogram. Authorities have also warned importers against artificially inflating prices.

But Nasirin warned that it’s not enough, and says prolonged economic pressure on small businesses could have wider social consequences.

“If things continue like this and the government ignores the issue, it’s not impossible that riots akin to the 1998 crisis in Indonesia could happen again. I appeal to the government to pay attention to this situation and take immediate action. I am only an elementary school graduate, yet I employ 40 to 50 people. If soybean prices keep rising and I am forced to shut down my business, what will happen to my employees?” he said.

The May 1998 riots in Indonesia were a violent, pivotal turning point triggered by economic collapse and hyperinflation, leading to widespread unrest and the eventual fall of President Suharto.

description: Hundreds of protesters gathered in central London as the UK government considers changes to permanent residency rules for migrant care workers, including proposals that could extend the waiting time for Indefinite Leave to Remain.

Footage shows demonstrators marching through central London towards Downing Street in Westminster, carrying banners and chanting slogans. Signs reading ‘Migrant life matters’ and ‘We care for your families, ours need security too’ can be seen as the crowd gathered outside the government buildings.

“We're here to speak to the ministers, to listen to us about the visa's requirements,” said care worker Tammy. “We come here legally. We pay 1000s of pounds to access the country. We come in, we pay tax, we do our work. We are basically the workforce, and then you tend to change the rules midway.”

“We've got a system at the moment that ticks every box in modern slavery,” said fellow care worker Adekole. “A system that allows people to be treated as slaves, to be treated as second-class citizens of the world, is not a fair system at all.”

Under proposals being considered in Westminster, the standard qualifying period for Indefinite Leave to Remain, or ILR, could be doubled from five to ten years.

The plans also suggest that individuals who access certain public benefits for a short period could face an extended qualifying period of up to 15 years, while long-term reliance could increase the requirement to as much as 20 years.

The proposals have been criticised by unions and parts of the care sector, who warn they could increase the risk of workplace exploitation and deepen staffing pressures and disrespect in social care.

“Nothing is given to us, let alone just respect. And dignity. We are not. We've had slurs, racist slurs, in our places of work. We've been called monkeys. We've been called, you know, 'gorillas' and 'apes'. We've been told to go back to the forest where we came from,” care worker Lydia said.

Supporters of the changes argue they are intended to reduce migration levels and ease pressure on public services and government finances.

video281
description: Coastal communities on Ontoloe Island, in Indonesia’s East Nusa Tenggara province, are turning shallow tropical waters into a marine farm, growing seaweed that helps sustain local livelihoods. 
Footage shows farmers tying young seaweed strands to ropes by hand before lowering them into warm, sunlit waters. The crop needs no soil, freshwater or fertiliser, just time, tide and steady care. 
“We release the seedlings tied to the ropes,” one farmer explained. “From small bundles, it grows into a much larger harvest within two months.” 
Once collected, the seaweed is spread out under the sun to dry, then bundled for sale. 
For many families, it has become a vital source of income in coastal areas where fishing alone can be unpredictable. 
“We harvest every two months,” one farmer said. “After that, we dry it in the sun so it can be sold at around 10,000 rupiah per kilogram.” 
Indonesia is one of the world’s major producers of tropical seaweed, much of it grown by smallholder farmers across the archipelago. Red seaweed varieties such as Eucheuma and Kappaphycus are widely farmed for carrageenan, while Gracilaria is used to produce agar. 
The dried seaweed is usually sold through local collectors before moving into regional processing and export chains. Indonesia exports large volumes of dried seaweed to markets including China and South Korea, where it can be processed for use in food production, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals and laboratory research.

video285
description: The United States launched another wave of strikes on Iran on Wednesday night, hitting surveillance, communications and air defence sites after an American Apache helicopter went down near the coast of Oman. 
Footage released by CENTCOM shows Tomahawk cruise missiles firing from the USS Michael Murphy at an undisclosed location. 
US Central Command said the June 10 strikes were ordered by President Donald Trump. It said Marine Corps, Air Force and Navy assets used precision munitions against Iranian targets which Washington said threatened US forces and commercial shipping. 
Hours before the strikes, Trump issued an ultimatum on Truth Social, linking the escalation to stalled talks over Iran’s highly enriched uranium stockpile. 
"Iran has taken too long to negotiate a deal that would have been great for them, now they will have to pay the price!!!" he wrote. 
The first US strikes came on June 9, after the Apache incident. CENTCOM said two crew members were rescued within about two hours and were in stable condition. It said the cause was under investigation, while later US statements blamed Iran for the downing. 
Iranian media reported explosions and projectile strikes across parts of Hormozgan province, including Sirik, Qeshm Island and Minab. Air defence systems were also reported active in Bandar Abbas, Qeshm and Sirik. 
Tehran has declared the Strait of Hormuz closed to vessel traffic after the US strikes. The waterway is one of the world’s most important routes for oil and gas shipments, and the announcement pushed oil prices higher. 
CENTCOM rejected Iran’s claim that traffic had stopped, saying commercial ships were still moving through the strait. It also denied Iranian state media reports that US warships had been hit by missiles and drones near the waterway. 
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it had retaliated against US-linked targets in the region, including the US Fifth Fleet in Bahrain and the Ali Al Salem airbase in Kuwait. Authorities in Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan said projectiles were intercepted without casualties. 
The exchange has pushed Washington and Tehran into a more direct confrontation, after months of pressure around the Strait of Hormuz and fragile diplomatic efforts. Mediation with Iranian officials has continued, but the latest strikes have left less room for an immediate off-ramp.

video292
description: Rio de Janeiro is pushing to become one of Latin America’s main artificial intelligence hubs, with plans for a vast new data centre complex at the city’s Olympic Park.

Footage filmed on Wednesday shows the area where the Rio AI City project is planned.

The project was announced during Web Summit Rio, one of the region’s biggest technology gatherings, with city officials hoping to draw billions of dollars in investment over the next decade.

"The project costs 500 million dollars to launch, and 10 billion dollars in total to build a data centre that will reach 3 gigawatts in the next decade,"  said Eduardo Cavalieri, mayor of Rio de Janeiro.

The city says the project is not only about technology, but also control over Brazil’s digital infrastructure.

"When we talk about data centres and infrastructure here in Rio de Janeiro, I even put on my Brazilian coat, we talk about sovereignty. This is the most important project of infrastructure sovereignty, of digital sovereignty in Brazil," Cavalieri noted.

During Web Summit, Rio signed a memorandum of understanding with Alessandro Lombardi, CEO of Elea, one of Brazil’s main digital infrastructure platforms.

Rio AI City is expected to attract around 65 billion dollars in investment and create more than 10,000 specialised jobs.

But the scale of the project has raised questions about its environmental and energy impact.

"Every time a data center is installed, a lot of water is used and stored in a closed circuit for cooling, but I don't know if this is the worst. In Brazil, we have an even bigger problem: we use a lot of water to generate electricity, and therefore, the question arises of where the electricity is directed," said Bernardo Costa, Professor at the Getulio Vargas Foundation.

Costa also urged caution over expectations that artificial intelligence alone can close the gap between developing and developed economies.

"I wouldn't say that, just because we are a developing country and invest everything in AI, we will get closer to the so-called developed countries," he said.

The memorandum between Rio and Elea is valid for 25 months and sets out a joint agenda to support Rio AI City, including institutional coordination and resource mobilisation.

CGT Union spokesperson Matthieu Bolle Reddat pointed to 'resignations, burnout and numerous sick leaves' as clear signs of the distress faced by the workforce. 
"These 13 suicides, which are only the beginning, are because many people confide in us about their suffering, their difficulties, and their unhappiness. They no longer recognise the company they work for," Reddat said. 
Sud Rail's Fabien Villedieu cited declining morale and safety, stressing rising layoffs and accidents are key indicators that employees are on the brink amid job insecurity. 
"There were 1,800 layoffs in 2025, a 15 percent increase; workplace accidents have skyrocketed by 20 percent, and now we’ve had 13 suicides since the start of the year, that's one suicide every 12 days," Villedieu added. 
Footage shows protesters marching through the capital waving flares, flags, and signs, as police monitored the demonstration. 
It comes after France has seen repeated nationwide strikes in recent years, particularly over pension reform. 
The state rail operator SNCF has gradually liberalised in line with EU rules, opening rail services to competition, which unions say has increased pressure on staff and eroded working conditions. 
Meanwhile, protesters also opposed the French government's refusal to nationalise ArcelorMittal's French sites, amid concerns over potential job losses. 
ArcelorMittal remains one of Europe's largest steel producers with major operations in France and has faced ongoing uncertainty due to global competition, uneven demand and rising costs.

description: The Nigerian National Museum in Lagos is allowing visitors to see, and in some cases touch, returned Benin Bronzes and other cultural artefacts taken during colonial rule. 
Footage captured on Tuesday shows an exhibition of ancient artefacts, including works from the historic Nigerian kingdoms of Benin and Ife. Visitors were seen walking through the galleries, looking closely at the returned pieces. 
"Some countries have been magnanimous enough to return those objects that were stolen, mostly the ones that were carted away in the 1897 expedition. So, as it is now, we are urging other museums across the world to help return those artefacts to us because we have the spaces to put them, and we can protect them," a visitor said. 
"Those artefacts, those works were not freely given. They are old. They are our own culture, our own cultural materials. But they were carted away in a horrible situation. They killed the men, and then they did all sorts, and they took those things away," added a second. 
The exhibition focused on artefacts taken during the colonial period, including the 1897 British expedition to the Kingdom of Benin, which led to the removal of thousands of bronze plaques, sculptures and ceremonial objects that are now spread across museums worldwide. 
Nigeria has long called for their return, saying the artefacts are central to its cultural identity. 
While some museums in Europe and the US have begun returning, or pledging to return, selected pieces, Nigerian officials say progress remains slow and incomplete.

"I always come back every June, every year because of the town fiesta and football," Nestor Parson, a former footballer, shared. "I've been in Toronto for 54 years, but I always return for the fiesta and the football."

The vibrant celebration, held from June 6 to 13, features spirited football tournaments, cultural street dances, and festivities. 
Barotac Nuevo's fiesta, closely tied to football, remains a cherished local tradition. 
The festival's name traces back to Tamasak, a prized white stallion owned by Don Simon Raymundo Protacio Belen. In 1811, he traded the horse to Spanish officials in exchange for his village, Barrio Malutac, being recognised as an independent town, later chartered as Barotac Nuevo. 
The 2026 FIFA World Cup is set to begin on June 11 in Mexico. The tournament will be played across the United States, Canada, and Mexico in an expanded 48-team format.

For many, this enchanting display rekindles cherished childhood memories, as fireflies have become rare in increasingly urbanised areas.

"What struck me most is knowing that fireflies are disappearing in many places," Yiyi reflected. "Being here felt like a nostalgic return to my childhood."

Yiyi highly recommends the garden's nighttime tours, highlighting the unique opportunity to reconnect with nature.

"It's hard to find places where fireflies gather like this anymore. I would definitely urge friends to experience the night tours at the botanical garden."

The region's warm, humid climate offers ideal conditions for these glowing insects, making it a magical destination for nature lovers.

description: Hundreds of people took to the streets of Sao Paulo on Tuesday night to protest against PDL 3/2025, a controversial bill critics have dubbed the 'PDL of Paedophilia.'

Footage shows demonstrators marching through the city carrying banners and placards reading ‘A child is not a mother’ and ‘Hands off our right to legal abortion’.

“At this moment we are living through – marked by imperialism and attacks on women around the world amid this situation of war – our country would be no different. We are seeing women's rights being attacked, including the few rights that the Constitution has guaranteed,” one protester said.

The demonstration came after Brazil's Federal Senate approved PDL 3/2025 on 2 June, revoking Resolution 258 of the National Council for the Rights of the Child and Adolescent (Conanda).

The resolution had established guidelines for the care and protection of children and adolescents who are victims of sexual violence.

The move sparked strong criticism from feminist organisations and human rights groups, which argue that it creates additional barriers for minors seeking access to legal abortion services in cases already permitted under Brazilian law.

“It further hinders humane care in cases already provided for by law. When girls and women have the right to terminate a pregnancy resulting from this abuse, from this violence, then this bill is suspending their right to humane care for these girls, for these minors,” said protester Tamires.

Supporters of the measure argue that the Conanda resolution exceeded its authority, bypassed parental consent and placed insufficient emphasis on the rights of the unborn.

The bill was approved by the Chamber of Deputies in a fast-track vote. As a legislative decree, it does not require presidential approval and proceeds directly to promulgation.

Organisers said similar demonstrations were planned in several other Brazilian cities, including Fortaleza, Pelotas and Vitoria.

Tensions between Taiwan and China - which regards the island as part of its territory under the One China principle - have escalated in recent months. "When we told you they would be there for a relatively short time, they were there for a short time, and it was handled with complete transparency. That is our trademark."

Under a bilateral agreement, the DRC agreed to temporarily host deportees from the US, with Washington covering all technical and logistical support. The first group reportedly comprised seven women and eight men from Peru, Colombia, and Ecuador. 

As a part of its current crackdown on immigration, the US has also sent deportees to other African countries, Uganda, Ghana, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea and South Sudan.

"It was like an alarm went off for us when we said, 'But okay, we can give our opinion, but from there to deciding the treatment my dad should have in an emergency moment, no," the woman noted.

Maradona died on November 25, 2020, due to cardiorespiratory arrest and pulmonary oedema while recovering from neurosurgery in a house in the locality of Tigre, about 50 kilometres north of Buenos Aires.

The judicial process is examining the responsibilities of the medical team and the circumstances under which Maradona's home hospitalisation was conducted, which was managed by the pre-paid medical company Swiss Medical.

The trial is also seeking to establish whether negligence played a role in the care Maradona received before his death. Doctors, nurses and other health professionals are charged with 'simple homicide with eventual intent' in the oral proceedings.

"This pink colour is natural. Some studies indicate that it is the normal microflora of the mother panda’s saliva. This demonstrates that the mother panda not only protects her cub physically, but when she licks her cub, she also protects it by maintaining the balance of microflora on its skin," he stated. 
Satrio Wiratama - Indonesian for 'brave and noble warrior' - was born on November 27 last year at Taman Safari, a conservation park about 70 kilometres south of Jakarta in West Java to 15-year-old pandas Hu Chun and Cai Tao. The pair arrived in Indonesia in 2017 as part of a 10-year conservation partnership with China, residing in a specially built enclosure at the park. Rio is the first giant panda ever born in Indonesia and the only giant panda born in a zoo outside  China in the past three years.

description: Analia Videla, an Argentine expert with over two decades of experience in the wine industry, has become Latin America's first certified water sommelier.

Through her unique role, Videla is helping to actively challenge the belief that all water tastes the same.

Footage captured in Mendoza on Tuesday shows Videla sampling water varieties while recording detailed tasting notes.

She explains that distinct geological origins and specific mineral compositions create vast differences between varieties.

"It is a rather mistaken concept that water is tasteless, odourless, and colourless. First, because it will depend on the origin. Water has terroir like wine. It has terroir because it comes from certain areas that have different geographical compositions," she explained.

Her fascination with the discipline began during her tenure as an international wine judge, when she noticed that different water profiles directly altered the palate of the wine and other beverages being evaluated.

"I started to pay more attention to the waters we chose for competitions because I noticed a big difference between those with a high mineral content and those that were more neutral," she stated.

This curiosity drove her to pursue training in Germany, where she found herself the sole Latin American representative.

"The limitation was that [the classes] were in German and I speak English and French. I said: well, the opportunity will come. And they contacted me last year to join the training group as the only one in Latin America," she recalled.

Videla admits that pioneering this niche profession in her region has brought a mix of skepticism and respect.

"People start to laugh a little, people who are ignorant of the subject. On the other hand, all professionals in the wine and beverage industry know how difficult it is to identify the attributes of other beverages," she pointed out.

Beyond refining the consumer palate, she stressed that understanding water profiles is vital for personal wellness. Essential minerals like calcium support bone density, while magnesium aids cardiovascular health and mental focus.

"It is important for health and also to break the paradigm that water not only hydrates but also nourishes," she assured.

Ultimately, the Argentine expert aims to dismantle prejudices and prove that water can be appreciated with the same depth as a fine vintage wine.

description: Thousands of devotees gathered at the Nampally Exhibition Grounds on Tuesday for the annual Bathini Fish Prasadam, a traditional practice where live fish are swallowed to treat asthma and other respiratory illnesses. 
Footage captured at the site shows vast crowds waiting in long queues to receive a live murrel fingerling stuffed with a secret herbal paste. 
Organisers struggled to maintain crowd control as attendees took turns to swallow the live fish. 
"I have a breathing problem and a cough. I need to go to the doctor regularly, and my grandfather told me about this place. So I have come here," one devotee said. 
Another explained that he had read about the procedure in local media. "There are people from all over India coming here to Hyderabad in Nampally Ground for this," he added. 
The annual event has been managed by the Bathini Goud family for around 181 years. The family claims the remedy was passed down by a Hindu saint in 1845 under an oath that it must always be distributed free of charge. 
To facilitate the event, the state fisheries department sourced and supplied the live murrel fingerlings, while volunteers pitched tents to provide food and water to those queuing. 
The Indian Medical Association (IMA) has repeatedly challenged the practice under the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act of 1954, while raising concerns over the secrecy of the ingredients. Independent medical research indicates there is no scientific or clinical evidence proving the efficacy of the treatment, with experts warning that swallowing live fish can pose choking risks or exacerbate existing respiratory distress.

Eskandari began her route in China before cycling through Vietnam, Laos, Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia.

description: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum announced on Tuesday the implementation of a decree suspending in-person work in public and private offices on 11 June, the opening day of the 2026 FIFA World Cup. 

The measure aims to minimise congestion on the roads of the capital, which is well-known for its heavy traffic.

The decree, published in the Official Gazette of the Federation (DOF), instructs Federal Public Administration agencies within Mexico City to transition to remote work as the tournament begins, Sheinbaum reported during her morning press conference.

"Luisa Maria is going to present a decree that was published today in the Official Gazette of the Federation to suspend work on the 11th in all public and private offices," the president stated.

She explained that the purpose of the initiative is "to avoid traffic and problems on the day of the World Cup." 

However, Sheinbaum clarified that the measure does not impose a mandatory shutdown across the entire private sector. "It is not an obligation," she emphasised.

According to the president, industrial production, manufacturing, and essential services will continue to function normally. 

"Stores, restaurants, diners, etc., will continue to operate. They have no problems," she added.

While the decree serves as a directive for federal government employees in Mexico City, exemptions apply to health services, national security, transport, social programmes and events tied directly to the organisation of the World Cup.

Educational activities will also pause, with classes suspended on 11 June across all capital city preschools, primary schools, secondary schools, upper secondary institutions, and higher education levels dependent on Public Education.

This comes as Mexico City finalises its preparations to host the World Cup's opening match between Mexico and South Africa. The other two Mexican host cities for the tournament are Guadalajara and Monterrey.

video371
description: Four Sumatran tiger cubs have been born at Taman Safari Indonesia II in East Java, in what the park has hailed as a major milestone for the conservation of one of the world's most endangered big cat species.

Footage captured in Pasuruan on Sunday shows a mother Sumatran tiger keeping watch over her four cubs inside a breeding enclosure.The youngsters, who were born in late March, can be seen padding between shaded areas and a water pool while remaining under close supervision.

Veterinarian Dr Nanang Tejo Laksono said preparations for the birth began long before the cubs arrived.

"We have been preparing for the birth right from the start. This included providing vitamins and special feed for both the male and female, as well as monitoring them from the very first mating to the last," said Dr Nanang Tejo Laksono.

"Once the mother became pregnant, we continuously monitored her and prepared a specific birthing enclosure equipped with CCTV to make surveillance easier. Alhamdulillah, they were born naturally," he added.

The litter consists of three males and one female, born to a male tiger named Praja and a female named Dini.

This is Dini's second litter. She previously gave birth to two cubs in 2021.

Park officials said the birth of four cubs is unusual, with Sumatran tigers typically producing litters of around two cubs.

Found only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra, the Sumatran tiger is critically endangered, with the Safari park noting fewer than 400 remain in the wild.

It is also Indonesia's last surviving tiger subspecies following the extinction of the Javan and Balinese tigers.

Taman Safari Indonesia II currently cares for 24 Sumatran tigers as part of its conservation programme, with the new arrivals providing a further boost to efforts to safeguard the species' future.

video375
description: The final group of nine female endangered white rhinos arrived at Zinave National Park on Thursday, completing a 48-hour journey and bringing an ambitious cross-border relocation project to a successful conclusion.

Footage filmed last week follows the rhinos on their 1,600-kilometre journey from Manketti Game Reserve in South Africa to Zinave National Park in Mozambique. Footage shows the animals being darted and loaded onto trucks before setting off on the long road trip, ending with a final farewell from the translocation team as the rhinos head out to explore their new home.

"It (Exxaro) made the decision to relocate the rhino for reasons of adding to genetic diversity in other countries but also to get the rhino away from high-density population groups and into conservation areas that are more secure," said Karin Ireton, independent non-executive director at Exxaro.

The transfer of the endangered animals from South Africa marks a major step in efforts to rebuild healthy black and white rhino populations in Mozambique and strengthen the country's broader biodiversity recovery.

"Zinave National Park had rhinos 50 years ago. And they were regionally extinct due to poaching pressure. So it was really important for us to get these rhinos back to their former habitat," said Kester Vickery, co-founder of Conservation Solutions.

Vickery described the operation as "one of the longest road translocations of rhinos ever attempted before". The complex undertaking required months of planning, specialised transport, technical coordination and round-the-clock veterinary support.

The newcomers join the park's existing white rhino population, bringing the total number to 39 inside the 4,080-square-kilometre reserve.

Park authorities hope the growing white rhino herd, alongside Zinave's 22 black rhinos, will establish the first viable founder populations capable of sustaining themselves in the wild.

The relocation was carried out by Mozambique's National Administration for Conservation Areas (ANAC), Exxaro Resources and the Peace Parks Foundation, with support from South Africa's Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment.

description: Every weekend, thrill-seekers gather in the misty mountains of Mount Arjuno-Welirang in East Java's Plembon for the 'Fun Race Gledekan' - a captivating sport-tourism phenomenon where racers zoom down steep, twisting hills on homemade, non-motorised carts. 
Footage captured on Sunday depicts hundreds of participants swarming the hilly roads that link the highland areas of Tretes and Palembon. They eagerly await their turn to take on the thrilling incline on wooden contraptions known as gledekans. These traditional Javanese wooden vehicles function as gravity-powered, non-motorised racing carts. 
The racing atmosphere transforms the tranquil mountain roads into a vivid spectacle of sound and sight. Spectators line the narrow, winding asphalt paths as the air echoes with the deafening noise of homemade carts racing side by side down steep gradients. 
Febri Kay, an enthusiastic participant, stated, "I play gledekan quite often; I’ve probably tried it around 10 times," adding, “The price for this gledekan equipment varies from 400,000 to 2 million rupiah (US$22 to US$110), depending on the customisation." 
Azila expressed her excitement, "This is the gledekan gang! I love this activity because it counts as a sport; it’s very unique and thrilling." She continued, "It’s special because, while it used to be made of wood, it’s now modernised with iron. I adore it for the adrenaline rush. I come every Sunday since that’s when many friends gather. It’s way better to be here than getting caught up in negative things." 
Without engines to propel them, drivers rely solely on gravity to achieve exhilarating downhill speeds, adding to the thrill as carts jostle for position through tight curves. Conquering the steep 500-metre descent demands extreme reflexes and courage, as these gravity sleds lack conventional braking systems. 
Drivers use basic hand-lever friction brakes or drag their rubber-soled shoes against the tarmac to navigate sharp corners, often leading to tumbles at high speeds, as seen during the Sunday event. 
Originating from a grassroots Ramadan tradition where village youths crafted wooden sleds for entertainment, gledekan has evolved into a major weekend attraction.
